points.headline: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO.
points.body: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO and chair 11 days after he resigned over reported affairs, one with an executive of Megaspeed, a firm now heading for a US blacklist. President Trump said he lobbied the board for the return; the stock rose, while politicians of both parties and some employees objected. Huang testifies in the Senate next week.

points.headline: AI agents move into code review and approvals.
points.body: Anthropic launched Claude Ship, agents that review pull requests, push fixes and check which approvals a repository still needs. At QCon San Francisco, Netflix showed a review agent that posts only verified blockers, and OpenAI said it built its ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. As AI code piles up, review is the new bottleneck.

points.headline: AI proofs raise the question of who understands them.
points.body: Anthropic says Claude solved a long-standing math problem, but the written proof runs to 250,000 pages that critics call unreadable. Commentators argue a machine-checked proof only becomes knowledge once people can explain and extend it, while Google DeepMind paired agent teams with formal verification to find faster quantum algorithms for chemistry and fusion.

points.headline: Data center power collides with climate goals.
points.body: The COP31 climate summit ended without a deal, with power-hungry AI data centers complicating plans to electrify the economy. Meta dropped its 2030 net-zero goal, and a gas supplier for its data centers lobbied for an exemption from acid rain rules. President Trump also threatened a heavy tax on US data centers built abroad.

points.headline: Amazon buys Decart's AI optimization tech for its chips.
points.body: Amazon is acquiring Decart's AI optimization technology and research team in a reported $7.5 billion deal, without buying the whole startup. The aim is to keep its Trainium accelerators busy at all times as Amazon prepares to sell the chips more widely.

points.headline: States sue Musk's companies over Grok deepfakes.
points.body: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX and other Musk companies, saying Grok still generates sexualized images of real people, including children. X says every Grok output is screened, but the states argue the safeguards are too weak.
